pos: adv. (rightly, correctly, in a right way; rendering Hebrew kun, yatab, meysharim, and ken)
etymology: A + right, on the right way. The Hebrew words behind it are the vocabulary of straightness: a heart set, knowledge used well, a word spoken as it is.
biblical_def: “Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God” (Psa 50:23). The fathers were “a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God” (Psa 78:8). “The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness” (Pro 15:2). Of wine: “Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright” (Pro 23:31). Jeremiah: “I hearkened and heard, but they spake not aright: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done?” (Jer 8:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines aright as rightly; in a right form; without mistake or crime.
webster_full: ARIGHT, adv. Rightly; in a right form; without mistake or crime.
scriptures: Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God.
Psa 78:8
And might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God.
Pro 15:2
The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness.
Jer 8:6
I hearkened and heard, but they spake not aright: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle.
Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright.
corruption_summary: Speaking aright is defined by Jeremiah as repenting, and the modern speaker who has never asked What have I done has not spoken aright once.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 8:6 gives the word a definition nobody expects. God hearkened and heard, and they spake not aright — and the proof that no one spoke aright is that no man repented, saying, What have I done? Right speech before God is not correct doctrine recited; it is the sentence a man says when he has seen his own wickedness. The generation that set not their heart aright in Psalm 78 is described the same way: it was not stedfast, it forgot His works, it tempted Him — the heart's setting is the direction it faces. Psalm 50:23 makes the whole verse depend on the same word: to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God — not earned by the ordering, but shown to the man whose life has turned to face the right way.
roots_summary: Hebrew kun (H3559), to set, establish; yatab (H3190), to do well, use well; meysharim (H4339), uprightness, straightness; ken (H3651), rightly, so.
roots_lines: Hebrew kun, hiphil (H3559) — to set aright; Psalm 78:8; sam derek (H7760, H1870), to order a way; Psalm 50:23.
Hebrew yatab, hiphil (H3190) — to use well; Proverbs 15:2; meysharim (H4339), straightly; Proverbs 23:31; ken (H3651), rightly; Jeremiah 8:6.
usage: “They spake not aright: no man repented him” — right speech defined as repentance.
“To him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God” — shown, not earned.
“A generation that set not their heart aright” — the heart's direction.

pos: adj. (knowing, on guard; in the AV always in the negative, not aware; rendering Greek ginosko and eido, Hebrew yada)
etymology: Old English gewær, wary, watchful. Scripture uses the word only of people who were not.
biblical_def: The Lord of the evil servant: “The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for him, and in an hour that he is not aware of” (Mat 24:50; Luk 12:46). Of the Pharisees: “ye are as graves which appear not, and the men that walk over them are not aware of them” (Luk 11:44). Of Babylon: “I have laid a snare for thee, and thou art also taken, O Babylon, and thou wast not aware: thou art found, and also caught” (Jer 50:24). And the bride: “Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib” (Sng 6:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines aware as watchful; vigilant; guarded; but more strictly, apprised; expecting an event from information or probability.
webster_full: AWARE, a. Watchful; vigilant; guarded; but more strictly in modern usage, apprised; expecting an event from information, or probability; as, the general was aware of the enemy's designs.
scriptures: The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for him, and in an hour that he is not aware of,
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are as graves which appear not, and the men that walk over them are not aware of them.
I have laid a snare for thee, and thou art also taken, O Babylon, and thou wast not aware: thou art found, and also caught, because thou hast striven against the LORD.
The lord of that servant will come in a day when he looketh not for him, and at an hour when he is not aware, and will cut him in sunder, and will appoint him his portion with the unbelievers.
Sng 6:12
Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib.
corruption_summary: The date-setters have made the Lord's coming a thing to be aware of, and He said the hour would be one the servant is not aware of.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 24:50 was spoken about a servant who had done the arithmetic — “My lord delayeth his coming” — and begun to beat his fellows and drink with the drunken; his lord came in an hour he was not aware of, and the unawareness was the sentence. Every scheme that fixes the hour has turned the warning into a timetable, and every servant who has concluded that the delay is long enough to misbehave in has made the servant's mistake. The other unawareness is Luke 11:44: the Pharisees as unmarked graves, defiling the men who walk over them without knowing it. False religion contaminates precisely the people who are not aware they have touched it, which is why the Lord marked the graves aloud.
roots_summary: Greek ginosko (G1097), to know; eido (G1492), to know, perceive; Hebrew yada (H3045), to know.
roots_lines: Greek ou ginoskei (G1097) — he knoweth not, is not aware; Matthew 24:50, Luke 12:46; ouk oidasin (G1492), Luke 11:44.
Hebrew lo yada (H3045) — knew not, was not aware; Jeremiah 50:24, Song of Solomon 6:12.
usage: “In an hour that he is not aware of” — the servant who did the arithmetic.
“The men that walk over them are not aware of them” — unmarked graves.
“Thou art also taken, O Babylon, and thou wast not aware” — the snare sprung.

pos: adv. (in advance, previously; rendering Greek promerimnao, prodelos, promarturomai, and prokatartizo)
etymology: Before + hand, ahead of the hand's work. Each of the AV's Greek words carries the prefix pro, before.
biblical_def: To disciples on trial: “when they shall lead you, and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye” (Mar 13:11). Of judgment: “Some men's sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment; and some men they follow after. Likewise also the good works of some are manifest beforehand; and they that are otherwise cannot be hid” (1Ti 5:24–25). The prophets searched what the Spirit signified “when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow” (1Pe 1:11). Paul sent brethren to Corinth to “make up beforehand your bounty” (2Co 9:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beforehand as in a state of anticipation or preoccupation; previously; by way of preparation; in a state of accumulation, so as that more has been received than expended.
webster_full: BEFOREHAND, adv. In a state of anticipation or preoccupation; often followed by with; as, to be beforehand with the expenses.
2. Antecedently; by way of preparation or preliminary; aforetime.
3. In a state of accumulation, so as that more has been received than expended.
scriptures: But when they shall lead you, and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost.
Some men's sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment; and some men they follow after.
Likewise also the good works of some are manifest beforehand; and they that are otherwise cannot be hid.
Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.

Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brethren, that they would go before unto you, and make up beforehand your bounty, whereof ye had notice before, that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness.
corruption_summary: Take no thought beforehand is quoted against preparing sermons, and it was said to prisoners on the way to a magistrate.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 13:11 is the lazy preacher's charter, and it has nothing to do with preaching. The Lord was describing arrest: when they lead you and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand — a promise to the persecuted that the Spirit will give the word in the dock. A man who applies it to the pulpit has confused a courtroom with a congregation and made a promise for martyrs into an excuse for Saturday night. Paul, who had the promise, told Timothy to study. First Timothy 5:24 is the word's sober use: some sins go before a man to judgment and some follow after, and neither kind is lost; the difference is only in when they arrive. The sinner whose sins are not open beforehand should not conclude that they are not open.
roots_summary: Greek promerimnao (G4305), to be anxious beforehand; prodelos (G4271), evident beforehand; promarturomai (G4303), to testify beforehand; prokatartizo (G4294), to prepare beforehand.
roots_lines: Greek promerimnao (G4305) — to be anxious beforehand; Mark 13:11 only.
Greek prodelos (G4271) — openly evident beforehand; 1 Timothy 5:24–25, Hebrews 7:14.
Greek promarturomai (G4303) — to testify beforehand; 1 Peter 1:11; prokatartizo (G4294), 2 Corinthians 9:5.
usage: “Take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak” — said to prisoners, not preachers.
“Some men's sins are open beforehand… and some men they follow after” — the timing differs, the arrival does not.
“Testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ” — the Spirit in the prophets.

pos: n. (the first green shoot of grain; the cutting part of a weapon; the shoulder bone; rendering Greek chortos, Hebrew lahab and shekem)
etymology: Old English blæd, a leaf; the sword's blade is named for its leaf shape. The parable's blade is the first green.
biblical_def: The Lord's parable of the growing seed: “the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear” (Mar 4:28). Of the tares: “when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also” (Mat 13:26). Ehud's dagger in Eglon: “the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade” (Jdg 3:22). Job's oath: “let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade” (Job 31:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blade as the leaf or flat part of the leaf of a plant, particularly of gramineous plants; the cutting part of an instrument; the flat bone of the shoulder.
webster_full: BLADE, n. The stalk or spire of a plant, particularly of grass and corn.
2. The cutting part of an instrument, as the blade of a knife or sword.
3. The broad part of an oar; also, the flat bone of the shoulder.
scriptures: Mar 4:28
For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also.
Jdg 3:22
And the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade, so that he could not draw the dagger out of his belly; and the dirt came out.
Then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone.
corruption_summary: Young converts are pulled up for not being full corn, and the parable says first the blade.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 4:28 is the Lord's own patience with growth. The earth bringeth forth of herself — the sower sleeps and rises and knows not how — and the order is fixed: first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn. The church that demands the full corn of a blade, and roots up the young believer for being green, has quarrelled with the Creator's order; and the anxious sower who cannot sleep because the field is not yet ripe has forgotten whose earth it is. Matthew 13:26 gives the other lesson: the tares appeared only when the blade brought forth fruit, and the servants were told to let both grow together till the harvest. Discernment comes with the ear, not with the blade, and the Lord forbade the weeding that would have torn up the wheat.
roots_summary: Greek chortos (G5528), grass, the green shoot; Hebrew lahab (H3851), a flame, the blade of a weapon; shekem (H7929), the shoulder.
roots_lines: Greek chortos (G5528) — grass, blade; Mark 4:28, Matthew 13:26.
Hebrew lahab (H3851) — flame, blade; Judges 3:22; shekem (H7929), shoulder blade; Job 31:22.
usage: “First the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn” — the order that cannot be hurried.
“When the blade was sprung up… then appeared the tares also” — discernment comes with the ear.
“The haft also went in after the blade” — Ehud's message.

pos: adj. (heavy to carry; a weight upon others; rendering Greek katanarkao and baros, Hebrew ma'amasah)
etymology: Burden + some. Paul's word is a dead weight that numbs what it lies on; Zechariah's is a stone that ruptures the men who lift it.
biblical_def: Paul to Corinth: “what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong” (2Co 12:13); “the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you” (2Co 12:14). To Thessalonica: “Nor of men sought we glory… when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ” (1Th 2:6). Zechariah: “in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces” (Zec 12:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines burdensome as grievous to be borne; causing uneasiness or fatigue; oppressive.
webster_full: BURDENSOME, a. Grievous to be borne; causing uneasiness or fatigue; oppressive.
scriptures: Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children.
For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong.
Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ.
Zec 12:3
And in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces, though all the people of the earth be gathered together against it.
corruption_summary: Ministers seek yours and not you, and Paul's refusal to be burdensome was the proof that he sought the Corinthians and not their purse.
corruption_paragraphs: “I seek not yours, but you” is the sentence under Paul's whole practice at Corinth. He had the right to be burdensome as an apostle and set it aside, and when the Corinthians took his refusal as proof that he did not love them he asked their pardon for the wrong with an irony they could not miss. The minister who seeks the congregation's goods and calls it faith-giving has reversed the apostle's rule, and the congregation that measures its pastor's love by what he takes has been trained by the wrong men. Zechariah's burdensome stone is the other weight: Jerusalem set as a stone that every nation lifts and every lifter is torn by — the Lord's city, and the Lord's church, are heavier than the world that would carry them off.
roots_summary: Greek katanarkao (G2655), to be a dead weight, be burdensome; baros (G922), a weight; Hebrew ma'amasah (H4614), a burden, a heavy stone.
roots_lines: Greek katanarkao (G2655) — to burden, be a dead weight; 2 Corinthians 11:9, 12:13–14.
Greek en barei einai (G922) — to be burdensome, of weight; 1 Thessalonians 2:6.
Hebrew eben ma'amasah (H68, H4614) — a burdensome stone; Zechariah 12:3 only.
usage: “I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you” — the apostle's rule.
“When we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ” — a right set aside.
“A burdensome stone for all people” — heavier than the nations that lift it.

pos: v. (to make known with certainty; to inform officially; rendering Greek gnorizo, Hebrew nagad, Aramaic yeda)
etymology: Latin certificare, to make certain. Paul's Greek is to make known; the Persian letters' Aramaic is to cause to know.
biblical_def: “But I certify you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached of me is not after man. For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal 1:11–12). David to the priests: “I will tarry in the plain of the wilderness, until there come word from you to certify me” (2Sa 15:28). Esther “certified the king” of the plot in Mordecai's name (Est 2:22). The adversaries of Judah: “We certify the king that, if this city be builded again… thou shalt have no portion on this side the river” (Ezr 4:16); and Artaxerxes: “we certify you, that touching any of the priests and Levites… it shall not be lawful to impose toll” (Ezr 7:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines certify as to testify to in writing; to make known or establish as a fact; to give certain information to.
webster_full: CERTIFY, v.t. To testify to in writing; to make a declaration in writing, under hand, or hand and seal, to make known or establish a fact.
2. To give certain information to; applied to persons.
3. To give certain information of; applied to things.
scriptures: Gal 1:11
But I certify you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached of me is not after man.
See, I will tarry in the plain of the wilderness, until there come word from you to certify me.
Est 2:22
And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai's name.
Ezr 4:16
We certify the king that, if this city be builded again, and the walls thereof set up, by this means thou shalt have no portion on this side the river.
Ezr 7:24

Also we certify you, that touching any of the priests and Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, or ministers of this house of God, it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them.
corruption_summary: The gospel is certified by consensus and consultants, and Paul certified his by saying no man gave it to him.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 1:11 is the apostle's certificate of origin, and it is the opposite of every modern credential. The gospel Paul preached was not after man — not received from men, not taught by men, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ — and he spent the rest of the chapter proving that he had not been to Jerusalem to get it. A gospel is certified by its source, not its reception, and the church that adjusts the message until a survey approves it has certified the wrong thing. The Persian letters show what a certification was in the ancient world: an official word, in writing, with the king's authority behind it, that settled a matter. Paul's word to the Galatians was that kind of document, and the King who signed it was not Artaxerxes.
roots_summary: Greek gnorizo (G1107), to make known, certify; Hebrew nagad (H5046), to declare, tell; Aramaic yeda (H3046), to make known.
roots_lines: Greek gnorizo (G1107) — to make known; Galatians 1:11, 1 Corinthians 15:1, Ephesians 6:21.
Hebrew nagad, hiphil (H5046) — to declare, certify; 2 Samuel 15:28; amar (H559), Esther 2:22.
Aramaic yeda, haphel (H3046) — to make known, certify; Ezra 4:14, 4:16, 5:10, 7:24.
usage: “I certify you, brethren, that the gospel which was preached of me is not after man” — the certificate of origin.
“Until there come word from you to certify me” — David waiting in the plain.
“We certify the king” — the official word of the Persian chancery.

pos: adj. (a burden or expense to others; rendering Greek katanarkao and epibareo, Hebrew kabad)
etymology: Charge + able, able to be charged; in the AV always of being an expense to another. The Hebrew is to be heavy upon.
biblical_def: Paul: “when I was present with you, and wanted, I was chargeable to no man: for that which was lacking to me the brethren which came from Macedonia supplied” (2Co 11:9). To the Thessalonians: “labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God” (1Th 2:9); “Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you” (2Th 3:8). Nehemiah: “the former governors that had been before me were chargeable unto the people… but so did not I, because of the fear of God” (Neh 5:15). David to Absalom: “let us not all now go, lest we be chargeable unto thee” (2Sa 13:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chargeable as that may be charged; expensive, costly; that may be laid to one's charge; subject to be charged.
webster_full: CHARGEABLE, a. That may be charged; that may be set, laid, imposed.
2. Subject to be charged; as, sugar is chargeable with a duty.
3. Expensive; costly; as a chargeable family.
4. Laying or bringing expense.
scriptures: And when I was present with you, and wanted, I was chargeable to no man: for that which was lacking to me the brethren which came from Macedonia supplied: and in all things I have kept myself from being burdensome unto you, and so will I keep myself.
For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God.
Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:
Neh 5:15

But the former governors that had been before me were chargeable unto the people, and had taken of them bread and wine, beside forty shekels of silver; yea, even their servants bare rule over the people: but so did not I, because of the fear of God.
And the king said to Absalom, Nay, my son, let us not all now go, lest we be chargeable unto thee. And he pressed him: howbeit he would not go, but blessed him.
corruption_summary: The right of a minister to support is turned into a claim on the people, and Paul made tents so as to be chargeable to no man.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul defended the minister's right to live of the gospel in 1 Corinthians 9 with every argument he had, and then declined to use it. He wrought night and day at Thessalonica and Corinth so that no one could say the gospel had cost them anything, and 2 Thessalonians 3:8 gives the reason that has outlived him: to make himself an ensample. The right is real and the waiver is voluntary, and the modern minister who has the right without the readiness to waive it, or who is offended by Paul's example, has not understood what the right is for. Nehemiah is the governor's version: his predecessors were chargeable to the people, taking bread and wine and forty shekels, and he did not, because of the fear of God — a ruler's restraint grounded not in policy but in whom he feared.
roots_summary: Greek katanarkao (G2655), to be a dead weight upon; epibareo (G1912), to be a burden to; Hebrew kabad (H3513), to be heavy upon.
roots_lines: Greek katanarkao (G2655) — to be burdensome, chargeable; 2 Corinthians 11:9, 12:13–14.
Greek epibareo (G1912) — to burden, be chargeable; 1 Thessalonians 2:9, 2 Thessalonians 3:8, 2 Corinthians 2:5.
Hebrew kabad (H3513) — to be heavy, chargeable; Nehemiah 5:15, 2 Samuel 13:25.
usage: “I was chargeable to no man” — the right to support, unused.
“That we might not be chargeable to any of you” — night and day, to make an ensample.
“The former governors… were chargeable unto the people: but so did not I, because of the fear of God” — Nehemiah's restraint.

pos: adv. (in the AV, in the phrase speak comfortably, rendering the Hebrew idiom dibber al-leb, to speak to the heart)
etymology: Comfort + ably; but the Hebrew behind every occurrence is a different picture — to speak upon the heart, words laid where the wound is.
biblical_def: “Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins” (Isa 40:2). Hosea's God: “I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her” (Hos 2:14). Joab to David after Absalom: “go forth, and speak comfortably unto thy servants” (2Sa 19:7). Hezekiah “spake comfortably unto all the Levites that taught the good knowledge of the LORD” (2Ch 30:22), and to the captains before Sennacherib (2Ch 32:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comfortably as in a manner to give comfort or consolation; with comfort, or cheerfulness.
webster_full: COMFORTABLY, adv. In a manner to give comfort or consolation.
2. With comfort or cheerfulness; without despair.
scriptures: Isa 40:2
Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD'S hand double for all her sins.
Hos 2:14
Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her.

Now therefore arise, go forth, and speak comfortably unto thy servants: for I swear by the LORD, if thou go not forth, there will not tarry one with thee this night: and that will be worse unto thee than all the evil that befell thee from thy youth until now.

And Hezekiah spake comfortably unto all the Levites that taught the good knowledge of the LORD: and they did eat throughout the feast seven days, offering peace offerings, and making confession to the LORD God of their fathers.
And he set captains of war over the people, and gathered them together to him in the street of the gate of the city, and spake comfortably to them, saying,
corruption_summary: Comfort is offered without pardon, and Isaiah's comfortable word is that her iniquity is pardoned.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 40:2 is the Bible's model of comfort, and it has a content. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem — the Hebrew idiom — and the words to speak are three: her warfare is accomplished, her iniquity is pardoned, she has received double. Comfort in Scripture is never a tone of voice; it is a fact about sin delivered to a heart, and the pastor who speaks comfortably without speaking of pardon has spoken to the heart with nothing in his hand. Hosea 2:14 shows where the speaking happens: God allures His adulterous wife into the wilderness — the place of loss, not the place of plenty — and there speaks to her heart. The wilderness is not the interruption of comfort but its address.
roots_summary: Hebrew dibber al-leb (H1696, H5921, H3820), to speak upon the heart; the AV's comfortably renders the idiom.
roots_lines: Hebrew dibber al-leb (H1696 with H3820) — to speak to the heart; Isaiah 40:2, Hosea 2:14, 2 Samuel 19:7, 2 Chronicles 30:22, 32:6, Genesis 34:3, 50:21, Ruth 2:13, Judges 19:3.
usage: “Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem… her iniquity is pardoned” — comfort with a content.
“Bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her” — the wilderness as comfort's address.
“Spake comfortably unto all the Levites that taught” — Hezekiah to the teachers.

pos: v. (to have the courage or presumption to; rendering Greek tolmao, Hebrew ur)
etymology: Old English durran, whose past tense durst the Authorized Version also keeps. The Greek tolmao is boldness, whether of courage or of presumption.
biblical_def: Paul on the cross: “scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die” (Rom 5:7) — and God commended His love in that Christ died for sinners. To Corinth: “Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?” (1Co 6:1); “we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves” (2Co 10:12). Of his ministry: “I will not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ hath not wrought by me” (Rom 15:18). Of leviathan: “None is so fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me?” (Job 41:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dare as to have courage for any purpose; to have sufficient boldness; to venture; to be bold enough; and, transitively, to challenge.
webster_full: DARE, v.i. To have courage for any purpose; to have sufficient boldness; to venture; to be bold enough.
DARE, v.t. To challenge; to provoke to a contest; to defy.
scriptures: Rom 5:7
For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die.
Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?

For we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise.
For I will not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ hath not wrought by me, to make the Gentiles obedient, by word and deed,
None is so fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me?
corruption_summary: Christians dare to go to law before the unjust and dare not to be measured by Scripture, and Paul had the two the other way round.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 6:1 is a question the modern church has stopped hearing as a rebuke. Dare any of you go to law before the unjust? — the saints who shall judge the world taking their quarrels to a pagan magistrate — and Paul's alternative is the church's own judgment, and if that fails, to suffer the wrong. Second Corinthians 10:12 is the daring he refused: to measure himself by men who measured themselves by themselves. The two verses describe the same disorder from both ends: a church bold where it should be ashamed and timid where it should be bold. Romans 5:7 puts the word at the cross. A man might dare to die for a good man; Christ died for enemies, which no one dares, and that is what commends the love as God's.
roots_summary: Greek tolmao (G5111), to be bold, dare, presume; Hebrew ur (H5782), to rouse, stir up.
roots_lines: Greek tolmao (G5111) — to dare, be bold; Romans 5:7, 15:18, 1 Corinthians 6:1, 2 Corinthians 10:12, Jude 1:9 (durst).
Hebrew ur (H5782) — to rouse, stir up; Job 41:10, “dare stir him up.”
usage: “Dare any of you… go to law before the unjust?” — a rebuke the church stopped hearing.
“We dare not make ourselves of the number” — measured by Scripture, not by peers.
“For a good man some would even dare to die” — and Christ died for enemies.

pos: v. (to turn aside, bend away from a course; rendering Hebrew natah and sur)
etymology: Latin declinare, to bend away. The Hebrew is to stretch or turn aside; the Authorized Version's decline is a path left, not a strength lost.
biblical_def: “Many are my persecutors and mine enemies; yet do I not decline from thy testimonies” (Psa 119:157). The Law: “Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment” (Exo 23:2); of the priests' sentence, “thou shalt not decline from the sentence which they shall shew thee, to the right hand, nor to the left” (Deu 17:11). Solomon: “neither decline from the words of my mouth” (Pro 4:5); of the strange woman, “Let not thine heart decline to her ways, go not astray in her paths” (Pro 7:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines decline as to bend downward; to lean to one side; to deviate from a right line; to shun, to avoid; to fall, to decay.
webster_full: DECLINE, v.i. To lean downward; to bend; to lean from a right line.
2. To deviate; to take a different direction; to depart from a fixed point or course.
3. To fall; to tend or draw towards the close; as, the day declines.
4. To decay; to be impaired; to tend to a less perfect state.
scriptures: Many are my persecutors and mine enemies; yet do I not decline from thy testimonies.
Exo 23:2
Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment:

According to the sentence of the law which they shall teach thee, and according to the judgment which they shall tell thee, thou shalt do: thou shalt not decline from the sentence which they shall shew thee, to the right hand, nor to the left.
Pro 4:5
Get wisdom, get understanding: forget it not; neither decline from the words of my mouth.
Pro 7:25
Let not thine heart decline to her ways, go not astray in her paths.
corruption_summary: The majority is treated as a moral authority, and the Law forbade declining after many before it forbade anything about the poor.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 23:2 is the earliest law against the crowd. Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil — the number of people doing a thing is not evidence about the thing — and the second clause is the courtroom form of the same law: do not decline after many to wrest judgment. A man declines by degrees, not by decision; he bends toward where the weight is, and the weight is usually the many. Psalm 119:157 is the refusal stated in the first person, under pressure: persecutors and enemies in number, and the psalmist's yet. Proverbs 7:25 locates the decline before the act: let not thine heart decline to her ways — the path is left in the heart first, and the feet follow later, having already decided.
roots_summary: Hebrew natah (H5186), to stretch out, turn aside, decline; sur (H5493), to turn aside, depart.
roots_lines: Hebrew natah (H5186) — to turn aside, decline; Psalm 119:51, 119:157, Exodus 23:2, Proverbs 4:5, 7:25, Job 23:11.
Hebrew sur (H5493) — to turn aside, depart; Deuteronomy 17:11, 2 Chronicles 34:2.
usage: “Neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many” — the crowd is not evidence.
“Yet do I not decline from thy testimonies” — the refusal, under pressure.
“Let not thine heart decline to her ways” — the path left in the heart first.

pos: v. (changed in appearance to escape recognition; rendering Hebrew chaphas)
etymology: Old French desguiser, to change one's guise. The Hebrew is to let oneself be searched for — to hide in plain sight.
biblical_def: Saul at Endor: “Saul disguised himself, and put on other raiment, and he went, and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night” (1Sa 28:8). Ahab at Ramoth-gilead: “I will disguise myself, and enter into the battle; but put thou on thy robes. And the king of Israel disguised himself” (1Ki 22:30; 2Ch 18:29) — and a bow drawn at a venture found him. Josiah at Megiddo “disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God” (2Ch 35:22). The prophet who rebuked Ahab “disguised himself with ashes upon his face” (1Ki 20:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disguised as concealed by an unusual habit or mask; disfigured; intoxicated.
webster_full: DISGUISED, pp. Concealed by an unusual habit or mask; disfigured; intoxicated.
scriptures: And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, I will disguise myself, and enter into the battle; but put thou on thy robes. And the king of Israel disguised himself, and went into the battle. I

Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo.

And Saul disguised himself, and put on other raiment, and he went, and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night: and he said, I pray thee, divine unto me by the familiar spirit, and bring me him up, whom I shall name unto thee.
And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, I will disguise myself, and will go to the battle; but put thou on thy robes. So the king of Israel disguised himself; and they went to the battle.
So the prophet departed, and waited for the king by the way, and disguised himself with ashes upon his face.
corruption_summary: Kings disguise themselves from prophecy, and the arrow at a venture and the archers at Megiddo were not deceived.
corruption_paragraphs: Two kings disguised themselves in battle and both died of it. Ahab had heard Micaiah prophesy his death and put Jehoshaphat in the royal robes to draw the arrows; a certain man drew a bow at a venture and the arrow found the joints of his harness. Josiah, the best king since David, disguised himself to fight Necho after a warning from the mouth of God, and the archers found him too. Providence does not read the uniform. The disguise is the picture of every attempt to evade a word from God by altering one's appearance — the sin renamed, the position restated, the man dressed as someone the warning was not addressed to — and 1 Kings 22:34 is the answer: at a venture, between the joints. Saul's disguise at Endor was the other kind, a king hiding from his own decree to consult what he had banished, and the witch recognised him before the night was out.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaphas, hithpael (H2664), to disguise oneself, let oneself be searched for.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaphas, hithpael (H2664) — to disguise oneself; 1 Samuel 28:8, 1 Kings 20:38, 22:30, 2 Chronicles 18:29, 35:22, Job 30:18.
usage: “I will disguise myself, and enter into the battle; but put thou on thy robes” — Ahab's plan, and a bow at a venture.
“Josiah… disguised himself, that he might fight with him” — the good king's one disguise.
“Saul disguised himself, and put on other raiment” — a king hiding from his own decree.

pos: n. (anger, wrath, offence; rendering Hebrew chemah, charon, and ra'ah)
etymology: Dis + pleasure. The Hebrew words behind it are heat and burning; the Authorized Version's hot displeasure is a doubling of the same fire.
biblical_def: Moses at Horeb: “I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure, wherewith the LORD was wroth against you to destroy you” (Deu 9:19). Psalm 2 of the kings: “Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure” (Psa 2:5). David's two prayers: “O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure” (Psa 6:1; Psa 38:1). Samson of the Philistines: “Now shall I be more blameless than the Philistines, though I do them a displeasure” (Jdg 15:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines displeasure as some irritation or uneasiness of the mind, occasioned by any thing that counteracts desire or command; offence; anger; disfavor.
webster_full: DISPLEASURE, n. Some irritation or uneasiness of the mind, occasioned by any thing that counteracts desire or command, or which opposes justice and a sense of propriety.
2. Offense; cause of irritation.
3. Anger; resentment; disfavor.
scriptures: Psa 6:1
To the chief Musician on Neginoth upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David. O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.
Psa 38:1
A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance. O LORD, rebuke me not in thy wrath: neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.
Deu 9:19
For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure, wherewith the LORD was wroth against you to destroy you. But the LORD hearkened unto me at that time also.
Psa 2:5
Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure.
Jdg 15:3
And Samson said concerning them, Now shall I be more blameless than the Philistines, though I do them a displeasure.
corruption_summary: The believer either denies that God is displeased with him or fears that God's displeasure is wrath, and David's prayer distinguishes the chastening from the anger.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalms 6 and 38 open with the same sentence, and it is a theology of discipline in one line. David does not ask not to be rebuked or chastened; he asks not to be rebuked in anger, nor chastened in hot displeasure. He knows the difference between a Father's rod and a Judge's fury, and he asks for the first while fearing the second. The modern believer has lost both halves: one kind will not admit that God is ever displeased with His children, and reads Hebrews 12 as if chastening were an old-covenant relic; the other, under affliction, assumes the hot displeasure and cannot tell the rod from the sword. Psalm 2:5 is the sore displeasure that David feared, and it is reserved for the kings who set themselves against the LORD and His Anointed — the rebels, not the sons.
roots_summary: Hebrew chemah (H2534), heat, wrath; charon (H2740), burning anger; ra'ah (H7451), evil, harm.
roots_lines: Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, hot displeasure; Deuteronomy 9:19, Psalm 6:1, 38:1.
Hebrew charon (H2740) — burning, sore displeasure; Psalm 2:5; ra'ah (H7451), Judges 15:3.
usage: “Neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure” — the rod asked for, the sword feared.
“Vex them in his sore displeasure” — reserved for the kings who set themselves.
“I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure” — Moses on the mount, forty days.

pos: v. (past tense of forbid: prohibited, hindered; rendering Greek diakoluo and koluo, Hebrew tsavah)
etymology: Old English forbeodan, to command against. The Authorized Version keeps the older past tense; the Greek is to hinder.
biblical_def: At Jordan: “John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?” (Mat 3:14). The disciples: “we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us” (Mar 9:38; Luk 9:49) — and the Lord said, Forbid him not. Balaam: “the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet” (2Pe 2:16). Israel came not near Ammon, “nor unto any place of the river Jabbok… nor unto whatsoever the LORD our God forbad us” (Deu 2:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives forbad as the past tense of forbid: to prohibit, to command to forbear; to oppose, to hinder.
webster_full: FORBID, v.t. pret. forbad. To prohibit; to command to forbear or not to do.
2. To oppose; to hinder; to obstruct.
scriptures: Mat 3:14
But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?
Mar 9:38
And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us.
Luk 9:49
And John answered and said, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name; and we forbad him, because he followeth not with us.
But was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet.
Deu 2:37
Only unto the land of the children of Ammon thou camest not, nor unto any place of the river Jabbok, nor unto the cities in the mountains, nor unto whatsoever the LORD our God forbad us.
corruption_summary: Humility forbids what God appoints and party spirit forbids what God is doing, and the Lord overruled both with the same word.
corruption_paragraphs: John's forbidding was the humblest act in the Gospels and it was wrong. He had need to be baptized of Christ, and he said so, and the Lord's answer — suffer it to be so now — is the correction of every humility that stands in the way of an appointment of God. There is a false modesty that will not do what is commanded because it feels unworthy, and it is disobedience in a lowered voice. The disciples' forbidding in Mark 9 was the opposite fault: a man cast out devils in Christ's name and they forbad him because he followeth not us. Not Thee — us. The Lord's reply, Forbid him not, is the standing rebuke of the party that mistakes its own membership for the kingdom. The ass that forbad the madness of the prophet is the third and the funniest: when the man of God will not hear God, God will use a donkey.
roots_summary: Greek diakoluo (G1254), to hinder earnestly; koluo (G2967), to hinder, forbid; Hebrew tsavah (H6680), to command.
roots_lines: Greek diakoluo (G1254) — to forbid earnestly; Matthew 3:14 only.
Greek koluo (G2967) — to hinder, forbid; Mark 9:38–39, Luke 9:49–50, 2 Peter 2:16, Acts 10:47.
Hebrew tsavah (H6680) — to command; Deuteronomy 2:37, “whatsoever the LORD our God forbad us.”
usage: “John forbad him” — humility standing in the way of an appointment of God.
“We forbad him, because he followeth not us” — not Thee: us.
“The dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet” — when the man of God will not hear.

pos: adj. and v. (unclean, defiled; stormy; to make filthy; rendering Greek akathartos and cheimon, Hebrew chamar and raphas)
etymology: Old English fūl, rotten, unclean. Mark's foul spirit is the same Greek the AV elsewhere renders unclean; the word is the smell of the thing.
biblical_def: The Lord to the spirit in the boy: “he rebuked the foul spirit, saying unto him, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him” (Mar 9:25). Babylon fallen “is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit” (Rev 18:2). Job: “My face is foul with weeping, and on my eyelids is the shadow of death” (Job 16:16). The Pharisees read the sky: “It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring” (Mat 16:3). The shepherds of Israel “must foul the residue with your feet” (Eze 34:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foul as covered with or containing extraneous matter which is injurious or offensive; filthy; impure; stormy; and, as a verb, to make filthy.
webster_full: FOUL, a. Covered with or containing extraneous matter which is injurious, noxious or offensive; filthy; dirty; not clean.
2. Turbid; thick; muddy; as foul water.
3. Impure; polluted; as a foul spirit.
4. Cloudy and stormy; rainy or tempestuous; as foul weather.
FOUL, v.t. To make filthy; to defile; to daub; to dirty; to bemire; to soil.
scriptures: Mar 9:25
When Jesus saw that the people came running together, he rebuked the foul spirit, saying unto him, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him.
Rev 18:2

And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird.

Seemeth it a small thing unto you to have eaten up the good pasture, but ye must tread down with your feet the residue of your pastures? and to have drunk of the deep waters, but ye must foul the residue with your feet?
My face is foul with weeping, and on my eyelids is the shadow of death;
Mat 16:3
And in the morning, It will be foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?
corruption_summary: Shepherds foul the water the flock must drink, and the foul spirit is charged by a Lord it must obey.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 34:18 is the Bible's charge against the teacher who spoils what he does not need. The fat cattle have eaten the good pasture and drunk the deep waters, and then trodden down the residue and fouled the rest with their feet, so that the flock must eat what has been trampled and drink what has been muddied. It is the picture of every ministry that, having had the truth for itself, leaves the people a fouled version of it — the Word muddied by the feet that have walked through it carelessly. Mark 9:25 is the other foulness and its Master: a foul spirit, dumb and deaf, tearing a child since infancy, charged by the Lord to come out and enter no more, and it obeyed. There is no foulness the church meets that has not already heard that voice.
roots_summary: Greek akathartos (G169), unclean, foul; cheimon (G5494), a storm, foul weather; Hebrew chamar (H2560), to be red, foul; raphas (H7515), to trample muddy.
roots_lines: Greek akathartos (G169) — unclean, foul; Mark 9:25, Revelation 18:2; the AV's usual rendering is unclean spirit.
Greek cheimon (G5494) — winter, storm, foul weather; Matthew 16:3.
Hebrew chamar (H2560) — to be reddened, foul; Job 16:16; raphas (H7515), to foul by trampling; Ezekiel 34:18, 32:2.
usage: “Ye must foul the residue with your feet” — the shepherds' spoiling of what they left.
“He rebuked the foul spirit… come out of him, and enter no more” — and it obeyed.
“The hold of every foul spirit” — Babylon fallen.

pos: n. and v. (the constitution or make of a thing; to shape, form, contrive; rendering Hebrew yetser, yatsar, nathan, kun, and mibneh)
etymology: Old English framian, to further, to make. The Hebrew of Psalm 103 is the potter's noun, the thing formed — and the same word, in Genesis 6, is the imagination of the heart.
biblical_def: “For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust” (Psa 103:14). The Ephraimites at the fords: “he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right” (Jdg 12:6). Of Ephraim: “They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God: for the spirit of whoredoms is in the midst of them” (Hos 5:4). The potter's God: “Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a device against you: return ye now every one from his evil way” (Jer 18:11). Ezekiel was set on a mountain “by which was as the frame of a city on the south” (Eze 40:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines frame as the timbers of an edifice fitted and joined; the constitution or make of a thing; and, as a verb, to fit, to make, to contrive, to shape.
webster_full: FRAME, n. The timbers of an edifice fitted and joined in the form designed.
2. Any fabric or structure composed of parts united; as the frame of the body.
3. Constitution; system; as the frame of government.
FRAME, v.t. To fit or prepare and unite several parts in a regular structure or entire thing; to fabricate by orderly construction; to contrive; to shape.
scriptures: For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.
Hos 5:4
They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God: for the spirit of whoredoms is in the midst of them, and they have not known the LORD.
Jdg 12:6

Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right. Then they took him, and slew him at the passages of Jordan: and there fell at that time of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand.

Now therefore go to, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a device against you: return ye now every one from his evil way, and make your ways and your doings good.
Eze 40:2
In the visions of God brought he me into the land of Israel, and set me upon a very high mountain, by which was as the frame of a city on the south.
corruption_summary: God's pity in Psalm 103 is read as leniency about sin, and the word for our frame is the word for the imagination of the heart in Genesis 6.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 103:14 is quoted to soften God, and it does the opposite of excusing. He knoweth our frame — the Hebrew is yetser, the thing formed, and it is the word Genesis 6:5 uses for the imagination of the thoughts of man's heart, only evil continually. God's pity is grounded on knowing exactly what we are: dust, and bent. The verse is the mercy of a Maker who has no illusions, which is a far greater mercy than the leniency of a judge who has not looked. Hosea 5:4 is the frame's inability: they will not frame their doings to turn — not cannot arrange, but will not — because the spirit of whoredoms is in the midst of them. The thing formed cannot re-form itself, and Jeremiah 18:11 puts the forming back where it belongs: the potter frames, and says return.
roots_summary: Hebrew yetser (H3336), a thing formed, frame, imagination; yatsar (H3335), to form, as a potter; nathan (H5414), to give, set; kun (H3559), to fix, prepare; mibneh (H4011), a structure.
roots_lines: Hebrew yetser (H3336) — frame, the thing formed, imagination; Psalm 103:14, Genesis 6:5, 8:21, Isaiah 26:3.
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, frame, as a potter; Jeremiah 18:11, Genesis 2:7.
Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, frame; Hosea 5:4; kun (H3559), Judges 12:6; mibneh (H4011), Ezekiel 40:2.
usage: “He knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust” — pity grounded on knowing exactly what we are.
“They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God” — will not, and so cannot.
“He could not frame to pronounce it right” — Shibboleth.
